subject: Civil Engineering
title: Tsunamis: Earthquakes at Sea
description: A micro-lesson that makes Tsunamis: Earthquakes at Sea usable.

hook.text: The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami killed 230,000 people — triggered by a magnitude 9.1 quake.

buildup.text: Subduction zone earthquakes thrust the seafloor upward — displacing trillions of gallons.

discovery.text: Tsunami waves cross oceans at jet speed — 500 mph — but are only inches tall in deep water.

twist.text: As waves reach shallow coast, they slow down and pile up — walls of water 100 feet high.

climax.text: Deep-ocean sensors now detect tsunamis and trigger coastal warnings within minutes.

punchline.text: The deadliest wave starts invisibly. Detection buys the minutes that save lives.

quiz.question: Why do tsunamis grow taller as they approach the coast?
options: Coastal winds push the waves higher as they approach land
Shallow water slows the wave, causing energy to pile up into taller walls of water
The seafloor rises and physically pushes the wave upward

details.summary: Tsunamis are ocean waves generated when underwater earthquakes vertically displace the seabed over large areas. They travel across oceans at jet-plane speeds with low amplitude, then pile up to devastating heights as they reach shallow coastal waters.
details.whyItMatters: Tsunamis extend earthquake danger far beyond the shaking zone, threatening coastlines thousands of kilometers from the earthquake source. Warning systems and coastal engineering save lives.
takeaways: Underwater fault displacement vertically lifts the water column above it
Tsunami waves travel at 700 to 900 km/h in deep ocean with minimal height
Waves amplify to 10 to 40 meters as they slow down in shallow coastal water

faq.question: Why can't you see a tsunami approaching in deep ocean?
faq.answer: In deep water, tsunami wavelengths extend over 200 kilometers while their height is only 30 to 60 centimeters, making them imperceptible to ships. As the wave enters shallow water, the front slows while the back continues at deep-water speed, compressing the wave energy into a much shorter.

faq.question: How do tsunami warning systems work?
faq.answer: Deep-ocean pressure sensors detect the tsunami wave passing overhead and transmit data via satellite. Seismic networks detect the earthquake within minutes and assess tsunami potential. Computer models predict arrival times and wave heights for all affected coastlines.
